title: Shania Twain's 'Little Miss Twain' Is a Love Letter to Her Childhood and Late Mother
excerpt: The country-pop icon's seventh studio album, out July 24, reflects on performing in bars at age 8, poverty in northern Ontario, and the mother who believed she'd be the next Tanya Tucker.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Shania Twain's album 'Little Miss Twain' releases July 24, featuring notable collaborations.
  • The album reflects on Twain's childhood and her late mother's influence on her career.
  • Twain began performing in bars at age 8, shaping her artistry despite personal challenges.
  • At 60, Twain embraces her changed voice and feels she is finally 'getting it right.'
A Tribute to Her Mother
›Album is an homage to Twain's late mother, Sharon.
›Sharon believed Twain would be 'the next Tanya Tucker.'
›Twain's mother struggled with depression and violence at home.
›Tragic loss: Sharon and Jerry Twain died in a car accident in 1987.

A Return to Country Roots

Shania Twain, the best-selling female country artist of all time, is releasing what she calls the most personal album of her career. "Little Miss Twain," her seventh studio record, arrives July 24 via Republic Records, produced by Zach Dawes.

https://x.com/FoxNewsEnt/status/2079678530082988076

The 15-track album marks a return to country music after years of crossover pop. Twain told CBS Mornings the project is autobiographical in a way none of her previous work has been.

"'Little Miss Twain' is me, now, looking back at my child's self and the journey that child went through, from starting out in those bars at eight years old, right up to when I got my recording contract in Nashville."

— Shania Twain, CBS Mornings

Three singles have preceded the album: "Dirty Rosie," an R&B-inflected groover; the title track featuring Tanya Tucker; and "Faded Blue Jeans," a bluesy collaboration with Queens of the Stone Age frontman Josh Homme. The War and Treaty also appear on "Take It to the River."

An Homage to a Mother Lost Too Soon

The emotional center of the album is a tribute to Twain's late mother, Sharon. Born Eilleen Regina Edwards in Windsor, Ontario, Twain was raised in the small town of Timmins by Sharon and adoptive stepfather Jerry Twain in conditions she has described as impoverished.

"My mother was depressed a lot of the time. She spent a lot of her days in bed," Twain recalled on CBS Mornings. "She lived off coffee and cigarettes that I would bring her in bed just to see if she was still alive. There was a lot of violence in the house."

Despite these hardships, Sharon believed fiercely in her daughter's talent, telling the young Eilleen she was destined to be "the next Tanya Tucker." That prophecy came full circle when Tucker — inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 2023 — agreed to feature on the title track. "This song is an homage to my mother, who believed with every ounce of her being that her daughter was destined to be the next Tanya Tucker," Twain said.

In 1987, when Twain was 22, Sharon and Jerry were killed in a car accident north of Wawa, Ontario. Twain put her career on hold, returning from Toronto to become guardian of her three younger siblings.

Performing at 8, Getting It Right at 60

Shania's Journey Through Music

Started performing in bars to support her family.
Late 20s
Landed her first recording contract.
Age 30
Released her first top-10 record.
1997
Released 'Come On Over,' best-selling album by a female artist.

Announces release of 'Little Miss Twain' on July 24.

Twain began singing in bars at age 8, performing cover songs to support her family. Those years shaped her artistry but left deep scars. "I was starting so young in bars that were smoky, and everyone was intoxicated. I don't know what I'm actually singing about, because I'm singing about divorce, and I'm eight," she told CBS.

She did not land a recording contract until her late 20s; her first top-10 record came at 30. Her 1997 album "Come On Over" became the best-selling album by a female artist in history. She has sold over 100 million records and won five Grammy Awards.

Now 60, Twain says age has allowed her to make peace with her past. "In my 60s now, I feel like I've really gotten it, or I'm just now getting all of that right," she told Fox News.

Embracing a Changed Voice

In 2003, Twain was diagnosed with Lyme disease, which damaged her vocal cords and led to a 15-year gap between albums. After open-throat surgery in 2018, her voice returned — but changed. "I have more of a fry to my voice, a little gravel. I've embraced it," she said. The Arts Desk called the album "more varied and entertaining than anticipated," praising its blend of country, R&B, and Memphis-style soul.

Full-Circle Moments

To promote the album, Twain has performed in intimate bars reminiscent of her roots — London, Toronto's Horseshoe Tavern, and Racket NYC on July 23 for SiriusXM, which is launching an exclusive pop-up channel through August 22.

"I grew up in Northern Ontario and the dream in my little bar bands was to play the Horseshoe Tavern. We weren't established enough. So this is my first time. I feel like it's a very full-circle moment."

— Shania Twain, Horseshoe Tavern, Toronto

nri_angle: Twain's story of overcoming poverty in rural Canada to become a global music icon, and her album's themes of honoring roots while reflecting on an extraordinary journey, resonates with diaspora audiences navigating their own connections to home.
